newsitem.title: GERMANY: German coffee market expects tight supply in 1997.
newsitem.headline: German coffee market expects tight supply in 1997.

text.p: Tightness fears expressed in last week's coffee price rallies dominate the German market although futures have temporarily reversed course in a downward correction, traders said on Monday.
They also said coffee retail price rises were looming across Europe, although each roaster was afraid to be the first to act and may try to push the deadline further.
"Nearby supplies are being snapped up as soon as they arrive so that the trade cannot rebuild its stocks and things don't look easier in the second half of the year," one said.
"The green coffee sector will remain a sellers market."
Feb/March afloat supplies from Central American and African origin countries were fast gathering value as consumers revealed some gaps in their short and medium term cover.
March/April arabica deliveries against the May futures position were also expected to be active.
"The industry now wonders where to look for suitable coffee for June/July," another trader said.
New York's March arabica futures, although lower at Friday's close at 136.90 cents, gained 10 percent last week.
This was caused by bullish crop and export supply fundamentals and the uncertain aftermath of a truck drivers' strike in Colombia, which had hampered exports.
Buying-in prices of green coffee against European currencies rose as outright prices and differentials advanced, accompanied by a firm dollar.
Roasters, who feel pressure on their operating margins, have acknowledged the need to raise retail prices.
But there has not been any follow-through after Bremen-based Eduscho lifted the price of one product last week.
Roasters fear announcements of price hikes could cost them market share in a market characterised by declining consumption and dwindling consumer appreciation of coffee as a valued item.
Importers reported sales of African, Central American and Asian arabicas, which rose by $14-16 on the week fob per 50 kg.
Brazils and Colombians were viewed as too expensive. They cost $154 and $170 at origin and $150 and $166 second hand respectively.
Jan robustas from Vietnam were offered at $71 cif, up $18.
